query_text: What impact modifier types and approximate concentrations are effective at restoring notched impact strength in PP compounds containing 30-50% post-consumer recycled PP to levels meeting automotive requirements?
draft:
Based on the provided excerpts, several types of elastomeric impact modifiers are effective at improving the notched impact strength of polypropylene (PP) and recycled PP compounds. These include ethylene-propylene rubber (EPR), ethylene-propylene-diene monomer (EPDM), ethylene-octene copolymer (EOC) or rubber, propylene-octene block copolymer (POBC), and polyolefin elastomers (POE) [Paper58, Paper172, Paper227, Paper51]. Ethylene-vinyl acetate (EVA) is also noted to improve the impact strength of recycled PP, though additions of up to 9% EVA still resulted in impact strengths lower than those of virgin PP [Paper168].

Regarding approximate concentrations for automotive applications, commercial formulations for car bumpers typically incorporate 10 wt% to 20 wt% of an impact modifier such as EOC, often balanced with 10 wt% mineral fillers like talc to compensate for stiffness losses (e.g., a 70/20/10 PP/EOC/Talc blend) [Paper227]. Other studies demonstrate that 5 wt% POBC [Paper58] or 20–25 wt% POE [Paper51] can significantly enhance impact resistance, and that metallocene ethylene-propylene elastomers are effective at increasing impact strength [Paper58]. 

However, the provided excerpts do not contain enough information to fully answer the query. Specifically, there is no data detailing formulations that use exactly 30–50% post-consumer recycled PP (PCR-PP) blended with virgin PP, nor the precise modifier concentrations required to restore that specific blend ratio to automotive standards. While the literature confirms that recycled PP from post-consumer containers can be modified with ethylene-octene rubber [Paper172] and that mechanical recycling degrades PP molecular weight [Paper227], the exact dosing requirements for a 30–50% PCR-PP blend are absent. 

To fully address the query, additional data is needed, including: the baseline notched impact strength of the specific 30–50% PCR-PP/virgin PP blend; the exact numerical impact strength requirements for the targeted automotive components (e.g., in kJ/m² or J/m); and empirical dose-response curves for modifiers like EOC or EPDM in that specific mixed matrix to determine the exact weight percentages needed to bridge the performance gap.
